opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest shift is in how analysts interact with information. For decades, the Bloomberg Terminal has been incredibly powerful, but it's also had a learning curve. You needed to know the right functions, the right query syntax, and where a particular dataset lived. Generative AI lets us meet people where they are: you can ask a question in natural language, and the system can figure out which data sources, functions, or documents are relevant and pull them together for you.

The second big change is synthesis at scale. Analysts are drowning in content: earnings call transcripts, filings, news, research notes. A lot of their job is reading, extracting the few things that matter, and connecting them. Models are now good enough to summarize a transcript, highlight what changed versus last quarter, or surface the key themes across a set of companies. That doesn't replace the analyst's judgment, but it compresses the time from "information exists" to "I understand what it means for my position."

That said, finance is a domain where the bar is very high. If a model hallucinates a number or misattributes a quote, that's not a minor inconvenience; someone could make a decision based on it. So much of our work goes beyond building the capability itself. We ground outputs in source data, provide attribution so users can click through and verify, and evaluate rigorously for faithfulness and accuracy. I'd say the experiences we can offer are fundamentally different now, but the trust and transparency around them matter as much as the raw model quality. That's where a lot of the interesting research and engineering challenges are.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think the honest answer is that it changes things in a couple of different directions at once.

The first thing to understand about Bloomberg is that our users are professionals who are extremely time-constrained. A financial analyst isn't browsing. They have a very specific question, they need the answer to be right, and they need it fast. So for a long time, the way we served that was through structured data and through a lot of very deliberately designed interfaces on the Terminal. Functions you learn, keyboard shortcuts, screens that are optimized for a specific workflow.

What generative AI changes is the interface layer more than anything else. Instead of needing to know which of thousands of functions to use, you can ask a question in natural language, and the system can figure out what data you actually need, go get it, and present it in a way that answers your question. So one big area is just reducing the friction between what someone wants to know and how they get there.

The second area, which I find more interesting from a research perspective, is summarization and synthesis over unstructured content. Bloomberg produces and ingests an enormous volume of text: news, earnings call transcripts, filings, research. No analyst can read all of it. So being able to say, "What are the key takeaways from this company's last three earnings calls, and how has management's tone shifted," that's a qualitatively new kind of experience. You're not retrieving a document, you're getting a distilled view that would have taken a human hours to produce.

But I'd put a big caveat on all of this, and it's where a lot of my own work focuses. In finance, being wrong is not a minor inconvenience. If a model hallucinates a number or misattributes a quote, that's potentially a real financial or legal consequence. So the experiences we can offer are shaped heavily by how well we can ground outputs in verifiable sources, show provenance, and make it clear to the user what's a retrieved fact versus what's model-generated synthesis. A lot of the interesting design questions aren't "what can the model do," they're "how do we build an experience where the user can trust it appropriately and verify it quickly."

So I'd say generative AI lets us move from giving people data to giving people answers. But the trust layer around those answers is what actually determines whether the experience is useful to a professional, or just impressive in a demo.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest opportunity is changing how analysts interact with information. They’re trying to answer questions that may require looking across earnings calls, financial reports, news, and market data. Generative AI can help bring those sources together, summarize what’s relevant, and make it easier to ask follow-up questions.

For example, you might ask, “How has this company’s discussion of risk changed over the last four quarters?” You could get a starting point for that analysis, with links back to the passages that support it, and then explore further.

But in finance, a fluent answer isn’t enough. The numbers have to be correct, the information has to be timely, and you need to understand where a claim comes from. So I think the interesting experience is one that helps analysts move faster while giving them the evidence and control they need to exercise their own judgment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it changes the way analysts can interact with information. They’re often trying to answer a very specific question, but getting to that answer can involve searching through filings, reading earnings transcripts, and bringing together information from several places. Generative AI gives us an opportunity to help with that synthesis, and to make the interaction more conversational. You can ask a question, inspect the supporting material, and then ask a follow-up.

The key, though, is that a fluent answer isn’t necessarily a useful answer in finance. You need to know where a claim came from, whether the information is current, and whether the numbers are correct. So I see the opportunity as helping analysts get to the relevant evidence faster and spend more time applying their judgment. That means building experiences where verification is part of the workflow, rather than asking someone to simply trust what the model says.
